title: How would you design a TAMPER-EVIDENT audit log (queryable, 1M events/day, 7-year retention) — make each record cryptographically chain to the previous one by storing `hash(current_record + previous_hash)` so any after-the-fact edit or deletion breaks the chain and is detectable, write to append-only/WORM storage, periodically anchor/checkpoint a signed chain head, and tier old data to cheap cold storage with an index for querying — why is a plain append-only table NOT tamper-EVIDENT by itself, and how does the hash chain close that gap?
shortTitle: How would you design a tamper-evident audit log

s1_definition.profdef: A tamper-evident audit log records every significant event so that any later edit, deletion, or insertion is cryptographically detectable. Each record stores a hash computed over its own content plus the previous record's hash, forming a hash chain in which changing any record changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so tampering cannot go unnoticed. The log is written to append-only or write-once-read-many storage, a signed checkpoint of the current chain head is anchored periodically so even a full-table rewrite is caught, and because the volume is high with long retention, recent data stays in fast queryable storage while old data is tiered to cheap cold storage with an index so it remains searchable. A plain append-only table is not tamper-evident on its own because a privileged user or a compromised database can still alter or delete rows silently; the hash chain and signed anchors are what make such changes detectable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a logbook where every page's corner has a wax seal made by melting together the current page's text and the seal from the previous page. If anyone tears out or rewrites a page, its seal no longer matches, and because each seal depends on the one before, every later seal breaks too, so the tampering is obvious. The logbook is kept in a vault that only allows adding pages, never erasing them, and every night the manager photographs the latest seal and signs the photo, so even if someone replaced the whole book, the signed photos would not match. Old logbooks move to a cheap warehouse but keep an index card so you can still find any entry. Just locking the logbook in a drawer, the plain append-only table, is not enough, because the branch manager with the key could still quietly rewrite a page; the seals are what make tampering visible.
s1_definition.oneliner: A tamper-evident audit log chains each record's hash to the previous one so any edit or deletion breaks the chain and later links, backed by append-only or WORM storage, periodic signed checkpoints of the chain head, and tiered cold storage with an index, because a plain append-only table can still be altered silently by a privileged user.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A tamper-evident audit log records every significant event so that any later edit, deletion, or insertion is cryptographically detectable. Each record stores a hash computed over its own content plus the previous record's hash, forming a hash chain in which changing any record changes its hash and breaks every link after it, so tampering cannot go unnoticed. The log is written to append-only or write-once-read-many storage, a signed checkpoint of the current chain head is anchored periodically so even a full-table rewrite is caught, and because the volume is high with long retention, recent data stays in fast queryable storage while old data is tiered to cheap cold storage with an index so it remains searchable. A plain append-only table is not tamper-evident on its own because a privileged user or a compromised database can still alter or delete rows silently; the hash chain and signed anchors are what make such changes detectable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a logbook where every page's corner has a wax seal made by melting together the current page's text and the seal from the previous page. If anyone tears out or rewrites a page, its seal no longer matches, and because each seal depends on the one before, every later seal breaks too, so the tampering is obvious. The logbook is kept in a vault that only allows adding pages, never erasing them, and every night the manager photographs the latest seal and signs the photo, so even if someone replaced the whole book, the signed photos would not match. Old logbooks move to a cheap warehouse but keep an index card so you can still find any entry. Just locking the logbook in a drawer, the plain append-only table, is not enough, because the branch manager with the key could still quietly rewrite a page; the seals are what make tampering visible.

**One line to remember:** A tamper-evident audit log chains each record's hash to the previous one so any edit or deletion breaks the chain and later links, backed by append-only or WORM storage, periodic signed checkpoints of the chain head, and tiered cold storage with an index, because a plain append-only table can still be altered silently by a privileged user.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the exact gap, because the question asks why a plain append-only table is not enough. An append-only table is a table you intend only to insert into, perhaps enforced by revoking update and delete permissions from the application role. That stops the ordinary application from changing history, but it is not tamper-evident, because tamper-evidence means you can detect a change after the fact, and an append-only table gives you no way to prove a row was not altered. A database administrator, a superuser, a compromised account, or someone with direct storage access can still update or delete rows, and nothing in the table itself reveals that it happened. The data looks perfectly normal afterward. So append-only controls who should change data under normal operation, but it does not detect a determined or privileged tamperer, which is precisely what a bank's audit log and regulators require.

The hash chain closes that gap by making the records mutually dependent through cryptographic hashes. Each record stores a hash computed over the record's own content concatenated with the previous record's hash, so the hash of record N depends on record N's data and on the hash of record N minus one, which in turn depended on all earlier records. This creates a chain where every record's hash transitively depends on the entire history before it. The consequence is that if anyone edits the content of an old record, that record's recomputed hash changes, which no longer matches what the next record hashed over, so the next link breaks, and because that next record's hash is now effectively wrong, every subsequent link breaks too. A single change does not stay local; it invalidates the whole tail of the chain, which is easy to detect by recomputing hashes and comparing. Deleting a record or inserting a fake one breaks the chain in the same way, because the previous-hash linkage no longer lines up.

Verification is the operational payoff. To check integrity you walk the chain from a known-good starting point, recomputing each record's hash from its content and the stored previous hash and confirming it matches the stored hash and that each record's previous-hash equals the actual previous record's hash. The first mismatch pinpoints where tampering occurred. This can be run continuously or on demand, and it needs only the records and the hash function, no secret.

But the hash chain alone has a weakness that the signed anchor fixes. If an attacker has full write access to the whole table, they could edit an old record and then recompute and rewrite every later hash, producing a new internally consistent chain. The defence is to periodically anchor the chain head: at intervals you take the latest record's hash, the chain head, and sign it with a private key or publish it somewhere the attacker cannot alter, such as a separate append-only store, a WORM system, a notary service, or even a public blockchain, and you keep these signed checkpoints. Now even a full rewrite is caught, because the rewritten chain's head will not match the previously signed checkpoints, and the attacker cannot forge a valid signature without the private key. The combination of the chain plus signed anchors gives strong tamper-evidence: local edits break the chain, and whole-chain rewrites fail against the anchors.

Write-once-read-many storage strengthens prevention alongside detection. Writing the log, or at least the periodic checkpoints, to WORM storage, which physically or by policy forbids modification and deletion for a retention period, means an attacker cannot even perform the edit in the first place on that medium, and object stores offer object-lock or immutability modes for exactly this. You combine this with append-only database permissions so the normal path cannot modify history, giving defence in depth: append-only and WORM prevent casual tampering, and the hash chain with signed anchors detects any tampering that slips through.

Now the scale and query requirements, one million events a day for seven years, which is on the order of a few billion records. You cannot keep all of that in a single hot, expensive, heavily indexed store, nor can you afford to lose queryability. The pattern is tiering by age: recent events, say the last few months that are queried most, stay in a fast, indexed, queryable store; older events are moved to cheap cold storage such as object storage, compressed and partitioned by date, with an index kept so you can still locate and retrieve any record by time, actor, or entity. The hash chain spans the tiers because each record carries its previous hash regardless of where it is stored, so integrity is preserved as data ages, and the signed checkpoints let you verify a cold segment without replaying the entire seven years. Partitioning by day also makes retention and legal holds easy, since you expire or lock whole date partitions.

Queryability is designed in rather than bolted on. You decide the access patterns up front, typically by time range, by actor or user, and by the entity or resource affected, and you index for those. For the cold tier you keep a lightweight index, for example in a search engine or a metadata table, that maps those query keys to the object and offset in cold storage, so a query first consults the index and then fetches only the needed objects. This keeps queries fast even though most data lives in cheap storage.

Senior nuances worth stating: use a strong cryptographic hash and include a record sequence number and timestamp in the hashed content so reordering is also detectable; sign checkpoints with a key held in a hardware security module or secrets manager so the anchor cannot be forged; batch the chaining and checkpointing so the one-million-per-day write rate is cheap, for example chaining per record but anchoring periodically; never let the application role have update or delete on the log, and audit even administrative access; and remember the clean separation of duties, append-only and WORM are prevention while the hash chain and signed anchors are detection, and a bank needs both. The headline point to deliver is always that append-only answers who may change the data, while the hash chain and signed anchors answer whether anyone did.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India logged every sensitive action, like Rajesh viewing Priya's statement or an officer changing a limit, into an append-only table, but an auditor pointed out that a database administrator could still silently edit a row to hide misconduct, and nothing would reveal it. This is exactly why append-only is not tamper-evident, and it is solved by chaining each record's hash to the previous one so any edit breaks the chain.

Problem 2 — The team worried that an attacker with full table access could rewrite the whole chain to make it internally consistent again. This is exactly the whole-chain rewrite weakness, solved by periodically signing the chain head and storing those checkpoints where the attacker cannot forge them.

Problem 3 — With a million events a day kept for seven years, keeping everything in a fast indexed store would be ruinously expensive, yet auditors must still query old events. This is exactly the scale-and-query problem, solved by tiering old data to cheap cold storage with an index while the hash chain and checkpoints preserve integrity across tiers.

Our mini-project builds a tamper-evident audit log core. The code appends hash-chained audit records, verifies the chain, demonstrates that editing a record breaks verification, anchors a signed checkpoint of the chain head, and shows a query by actor. The demo logs actions involving Rajesh and Priya and then detects a tampered record.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three sensitive actions logged in order, an officer viewing Rajesh's statement, the same officer raising Priya's limit, and Rajesh transferring fifty thousand rupees, followed by a signed checkpoint, a verification, and then a malicious edit.

Step 1: The first action is appended. Since it is the first record, its previous hash is the genesis value, and its own hash is computed over its content concatenated with that genesis hash. The record now carries both its previous hash and its own hash.

Step 2: The second action is appended with its previous hash set to the first record's hash, and its own hash computed over its content plus that previous hash. The third action chains to the second the same way. Each record's hash therefore depends on everything before it, forming the chain.

Step 3: A signed checkpoint is taken of the current chain head, the third record's hash, and stored. In production this signature is made with a protected private key and written to WORM or a notary, so it cannot be forged or altered later. This anchor is what will catch a full rewrite.

Step 4: Verification walks the chain from genesis, recomputing each record's hash from its content and stored previous hash and checking the linkage. All three records match, so verification returns true: the log is intact.

Step 5: A query by actor OFFICER-7 returns the two records that officer created, using the actor index. This shows the log is queryable, which in production uses the designed-in indexes and, for old data, a cold-storage index.

Step 6: A privileged tamperer edits the second record's content to inflate Priya's limit, but keeps the old stored hash. Now the record's content no longer matches its stored hash. Verification recomputes the second record's hash, finds it does not match, and returns false, pinpointing record one as the break. The tampering is detected even though the row was changed directly.

Step 7: Even if the tamperer had recomputed and rewritten all later hashes to make the chain internally consistent again, the chain head would differ from the previously signed checkpoint, and the anchor check would fail because the attacker cannot forge the signature. So both a local edit and a whole-chain rewrite are detectable.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    appended seq=0 VIEW_STATEMENT hash=3a9f1c2b8e04...
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    appended seq=1 CHANGE_LIMIT hash=7d41e0a6f2b1...
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    appended seq=2 TRANSFER hash=b2c8f33a19de...
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    ANCHOR: signed chain head = SIG(b2c8f33a19de)
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    verify (intact) = true
2026-10-24 15:12:10 INFO    records by OFFICER-7 = 2
2026-10-24 15:12:10 SEVERE  verify (after tamper) = false → tampering DETECTED
2026-10-24 15:12:10 SEVERE  anchor check = false → whole-chain rewrite also detectable
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Event: OFFICER-7 CHANGE_LIMIT on CUR3001
    │
    ▼
  HashChainLog.append(...)
    │ prevHash = hash of previous record
    │ hash = SHA-256( record_content + prevHash )   ← THE CHAIN
    ▼
  record[seq=1] { content, prevHash=H0, hash=H1 }
    │
    ▼  (append-only / WORM storage — no UPDATE/DELETE)
  chain: GENESIS → H0 → H1 → H2  (each depends on all before it)
    │
    ├─ every N records ─▶ CheckpointSigner.sign(head) → SIG(H2) → WORM/notary
    │
    ▼
  VERIFY: recompute each hash from content+prevHash
    intact → true

  ── Tamper (privileged user edits record 1 content) ──
  record[1].content changed, hash H1 kept
    verify recomputes → H1' ≠ H1 → BREAK at seq 1  (DETECTED)
    every later link also invalid (H2 hashed over old H1)

  ── Whole-chain rewrite (attacker recomputes H1'..H2') ──
  new head H2' ≠ signed SIG(H2) → anchor mismatch (DETECTED)
  attacker can't forge signature without the private key

  ── Scale / query (1M/day × 7y) ──
  hot (90d, indexed) ──age──▶ cold object store (WORM, by-day) + query index
  chain + signed checkpoints span tiers → integrity preserved as data ages
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A tamper-evident audit log records every significant event so that any later edit, deletion, insertion, or reorder is cryptographically detectable, and I always start by explaining why a plain append-only table is not enough. Append-only, enforced by revoking update and delete from the application role, controls who should change data in normal operation, but it is not tamper-evident, because a database administrator, a superuser, a compromised account, or someone with direct storage access can still alter or delete rows and the table afterward looks perfectly normal. Append-only answers who may change the data; it does not answer whether anyone did.

The hash chain closes that gap. Each record stores a hash computed over its own content plus the previous record's hash, so every record's hash transitively depends on the entire history before it. If anyone edits an old record, its recomputed hash changes, no longer matches what the next record hashed over, and every later link breaks, so a single change invalidates the whole tail and is trivially detected by walking the chain and recomputing hashes, with the first mismatch pinpointing the tamper. Deletion and insertion break the linkage the same way, and including a sequence number and timestamp in the hashed content makes reordering detectable too.

The chain alone has one weakness: an attacker with full write access could edit a record and then recompute and rewrite every later hash to produce a consistent chain. The fix is to periodically anchor the chain head by signing the latest hash with a protected private key, ideally in a hardware security module, and storing those signed checkpoints somewhere immutable like WORM storage or a notary. A rewritten chain's head will not match the previously signed checkpoints, and the attacker cannot forge the signature, so even a full rewrite is caught. I combine this with append-only permissions and write-once-read-many storage so prevention and detection work together as defence in depth.

For a bank's scale of a million events a day over seven years, which is billions of records, I tier by age: recent data stays in a fast, indexed, queryable store, and older data moves to cheap cold object storage with object-lock immutability, partitioned by day, with a lightweight index mapping query keys like time, actor, and affected entity to the object and offset so old data stays searchable. The hash chain spans the tiers because each record carries its previous hash wherever it lives, and the signed checkpoints let me verify a cold segment without replaying all seven years. On my project at National Bank of India this is exactly what we built after an auditor pointed out that our append-only audit table could still be edited by a database administrator with nothing to show for it; we chained each record's hash to the previous, signed the chain head every thousand records into WORM storage, kept ninety days hot and indexed with the rest tiered to a locked object store, and a continuous verifier job alerted the moment any link broke.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that tamper-evidence comes from chaining each record's hash to the previous one so any change breaks the chain and all later links, reinforced by periodic signed checkpoints of the chain head to catch whole-chain rewrites and by WORM storage to prevent tampering, all tiered hot-to-cold with an index for scale and queryability, because a plain append-only table only controls who may write and cannot by itself reveal that a privileged user changed history.
